My recommendation: fix collection loss in manual duplicate cleanup first, then simplify navigation and correct the search/duplicate vocabulary. Keep the warm palette, typography, masonry and metadata hierarchy. Retire legacy as a separate, bounded change with a real frontend-build gate.

Private review artifact: contains screenshots of your production library and local server configuration. Keep this report private; redact production media, hostnames, filenames and configuration details before any external distribution. All screenshots are embedded; it works offline without a running app or external assets.

Keep these strengths

  • Calm palette and clear title / summary / tag hierarchy.
  • Useful annotation-state badges and explicit NSFW visibility.
  • Working collection and metadata workflows in the sandbox.
  • Clear per-file partial upload success and explicit destructive confirmations.
  • Responsive layouts without document-level horizontal overflow at the widths checked.

What the report is—and is not

Three workflow problems were repeated: manual cleanup loses collection placement; Settings drafts disappear on navigation; Feed's “Back to library” can return to Settings. The other seven findings are design recommendations backed by observed screens and interactions.

This is not a claim of ten software bugs, a formal accessibility certification, or a complete video-playback test. Limitations are explicit below.

Showing all 10 findings.

UX-01 / Duplicates × CollectionsP1

Cleanup should preserve the places an image was saved

Reproduced workflow issueEffort: M

“Keep largest” deletes the smaller copies but does not move their collection memberships to the survivor. A tidy-up can quietly empty a saved collection.

What I observed

In the disposable sandbox, Audit scratchpad contained Cat duplicate variant B. Keeping the largest image in that duplicate group left Audit scratchpad empty. Repeated with a second group (Square companion / Dog portrait) with the same result. The confirmation names dimensions and deletion count, but does not mention affected collections.

Why it matters

People think of a duplicate cleanup as keeping the same picture in a better form—not removing it from their organization system. The existing warning says deletion is irreversible, but not what else disappears.

Suggested change

  • Make Keep largest a consolidation operation: union collection memberships onto the keeper before deleting copies, in one transaction.
  • Related improvement: preserve manual metadata deliberately; surface conflicts instead of silently choosing a winner.
  • Preview the keeper, number of removals, and affected collections. State whether files will be deleted or retained.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Save a smaller duplicate into a collection; confirm it appears there.
  2. Open Duplicates, choose Keep largest for that group, and confirm deletion.
  3. Return to the collection: the saved image is gone and the surviving copy is not in its place.

Done when: A collection containing any removed duplicate still contains the keeper after cleanup, with deterministic metadata handling and rollback on failure.

Repository issue: meta/issues/preserve-collections-during-manual-duplicate-cleanup.md

UX-02 / DuplicatesP1

Clarify what “Exact only” means

Design recommendationEffort: S–M

The words “Exact only”, “copies”, and “Keep largest” make a perceptual-hash match feel more certain than it is.

What I observed

The production view offers Exact only and labels groups as copies. In the first captured group, all five images are 450×424, but only the first is labelled largest. There is no visible explanation of ties or quality. The established feature contract is dHash equality/distance—not byte or pixel equality.

Why it matters

This is a destructive workflow. Hash equality, visual similarity, higher resolution, and better quality are different claims. The current labels blur them together.

Suggested change

  • Rename Exact only to Identical visual hash; call the groups Possible matches. Explain that colors, edits, and fine detail may differ.
  • Show an explicit Keep badge and let the user select another keeper. For equal dimensions say Same resolution, rather than implying one is larger.
  • Add file size/format and an accessible side-by-side comparison. On phones, offer a two-up/flip comparison instead of only a long vertical list.
  • Show the separate unattended-import policy/status when that feature is exposed in UI; do not imply the new import option fixes manual cleanup.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Open Duplicates and select Exact only.
  2. Inspect a group with equal dimensions and the keeper label.

Done when: No label claims byte equality without verification; users can identify the keeper and understand the deletion/retention policy before confirming.

Repository issue: meta/issues/clarify-perceptual-duplicate-safety-and-keeper-choice.md

UX-03 / Navigation & page layoutP1

Give mobile navigation fewer jobs

Design recommendationEffort: M

A phone gets the entire desktop rail as a row of tiny icons, followed by several more rows of controls before any media.

What I observed

At 390×844, the first media begins around y=373—44% of the viewport. Navigation buttons measure about 29×40 CSS pixels. Library and Collections use near-identical grid icons; disabled Tags and the legacy link consume space. Settings/Statistics/Collections also inherit the full search-and-tag band.

Why it matters

The visual system is appealing, but users must decode the icons, remember their destinations, and navigate small targets. Utility pages look like another library mode rather than a focused task.

Suggested change

  • Use Library, Search, Collections and More as the primary mobile navigation; move Statistics, Duplicates and Settings under More.
  • Use persistent desktop labels and a distinct Collections icon. Remove Tags (soon) until useful and retire the legacy escape link.
  • Collapse media/sort/NSFW options behind one clearly labelled filter control on small screens; retain a visible active-filter summary.
  • Use a compact utility-page header instead of repeating global tags/counts. Aim for comfortable 44px touch targets; this audit is not a formal WCAG conformance test.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Open the library at 390×844 and compare the space above the first image.
  2. Open Settings at the same width; note the same search/tag band above the form.

Done when: Proposed target to agree during implementation: labelled core navigation with 44px touch targets and first media within the top third of a 390×844 viewport, without losing filter discoverability.

Repository issue: meta/issues/simplify-atelier-navigation-and-mobile-chrome.md

UX-04 / Search, tags & countsP2

Make search modes and scope explicit

Design recommendationEffort: M

The tag pills look like refinements, but clicking one replaces the search. Counts and bare percentages add further ambiguity.

What I observed

Twice in production: search “a quiet forest at dawn” → 48 results → click Tag · outdoor → the query clears, heading becomes outdoor, and URL becomes ?tag=outdoor. Media/sort controls disappear in search. Results show bare 42%/39% badges. The library header's image/video totals and visible-result count have different, unexplained scopes.

Why it matters

A control visually attached to a search box is likely to be read as a filter on that search. “42%” can be mistaken for confidence or probability. Global totals beside the query can look like result totals.

Suggested change

  • Choose a clear model: additive tag filters with removable chips, or explicitly labelled Browse tag shortcuts separate from the search controls.
  • Preserve the query and filter scope visibly; make media filtering consistent between browsing and searching where supported.
  • Label similarity as a relative match score, or replace the raw percentage with rank/relevance presentation. Do not present it as confidence.
  • Distinguish Library totals from Visible results; use media/image/card consistently instead of pins and Quick collections for tag shortcuts.
  • Provide a visible Search by image button that opens a picker, especially for mobile and keyboard users; paste/drop can remain shortcuts.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Search for a quiet forest at dawn.
  2. Click Tag · outdoor under the search box.
  3. Observe that this replaces the query rather than refining it.

Done when: Users can predict whether a tag click refines or replaces a search; counts and match indicators identify their meaning and scope.

Repository issue: meta/issues/clarify-search-filter-scope-and-match-labels.md

UX-05 / SettingsP2

Protect unsaved Settings edits

Reproduced workflow issueEffort: S–M

A simple navigation click silently throws away the Settings draft.

What I observed

In the sandbox, changed the native variant from e4b to 26b without saving, navigated to Library, then back to Settings: e4b returned and Save was disabled. Repeated via Collections. There was no discard warning or retained draft. No model configuration was saved.

Why it matters

The same behavior can cost a longer remote-server configuration edit. Global search and tag links remain prominent while editing, making accidental departure easy.

Suggested change

  • Add a dirty-state guard with Stay / Discard changes, or retain an explicit unsaved draft across internal navigation.
  • Keep a Save changes / Discard bar near edited controls, and show a clear Saved confirmation.
  • Related layout improvement: avoid equal-height Settings cards that create a large empty backend panel; use independent panels or a compact form layout.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Settings → change a field; do not save.
  2. Choose Library or Collections, then return to Settings.
  3. The prior value is restored without warning.

Done when: Leaving a dirty form cannot silently erase edits; the user can distinguish draft, saved, and active worker configuration.

Repository issue: meta/issues/protect-unsaved-atelier-settings-edits.md

UX-06 / Lightbox & metadataP2

Separate viewing actions from editing actions

Design recommendationEffort: S–M

Save, Save to collection, Find similar, re-annotation and deletion compete in the same small action area—even during editing.

What I observed

The desktop editor shows Save to collection beside Save, then Cancel / Find similar / Open original / Flag NSFW / Re-annotate / Delete. On mobile, a long hash filename and description push these actions below the visible sheet. Actual title/tag editing and saving succeeded in the sandbox.

Why it matters

Two different “save” concepts compete, and unrelated actions distract from finishing the edit. A filename that is mostly a hash has little reading value but consumes prime mobile space.

Suggested change

  • During editing, emphasize Save changes and Cancel; move unrelated actions out of the edit flow.
  • In viewing mode, prioritize Save to collection, Similar, and More; keep destructive/reprocessing actions in the latter.
  • Make a compact action row sticky within the mobile sheet and collapse filename/technical fields under File details.
  • Retain the current title/summary/description hierarchy and previous/next navigation—they are useful.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Open an image and choose Edit.
  2. Compare the action area with the phone lightbox's initial viewport.

Done when: Save changes is unambiguous and reachable; core viewing actions remain easy to find without reading the entire description.

Repository issue: meta/issues/simplify-lightbox-actions-and-edit-mode.md

UX-07 / CollectionsP2

Make Collections feel like saved media

Design recommendationEffort: M

The collection index resembles a settings list: names and management buttons, but no visual memory cues or counts.

What I observed

Populated and empty collections look alike in the list. Rename/Delete occupy much of each row. The empty-detail state says items might be NSFW-hidden even for a genuinely empty list, and offers no direct Browse library action. Create, save, rename and delete worked in the sandbox.

Why it matters

Collections are a visual recall tool. Without a cover or count, users must remember what every name contains; management receives more emphasis than opening content.

Suggested change

  • Add a small cover mosaic and item count; make the whole card a clearly clickable browse target.
  • Move Rename/Delete into a labelled overflow menu while keeping delete confirmation and the promise that originals are retained.
  • Distinguish No saved items yet from Items hidden by filters, with Browse library or Show hidden items as appropriate.
  • Keep saved ordering stable and show short confirmation when a picker adds/removes an item.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Open Collections with one populated and one empty list.
  2. Open the empty list and inspect its next-step guidance.

Done when: A user can distinguish populated/empty/filtered collections at a glance and reach the next useful action directly.

Repository issue: meta/issues/improve-collection-browsing-and-empty-states.md

UX-08 / Statistics & error recoveryP2

Turn operational states into next steps

Design recommendationEffort: S–M

Scheduler vocabulary and generic errors tell users something happened, but not what it means or how to recover.

What I observed

Production Statistics shows queued and ready counts together, plus 468 videos needing a transcription job with none queued. It does not explain whether transcription is unavailable or simply incomplete. An injected local search-network failure displayed Failed to fetch twice, without Retry.

Why it matters

“Ready” sounds completed to a non-operator. An empty progress bar without an explanation can look broken even when a feature is intentionally disabled. Raw fetch errors do not offer a recovery path.

Suggested change

  • Use Waiting / Processing / Complete / Failed as primary states; explain scheduler subsets under Advanced details.
  • Show Not configured / Disabled / No audio when applicable, rather than implying every video has missing work.
  • Label totals that include sampled video frames, and distinguish them from standalone media counts.
  • Use one plain-language error with Retry preserving the query/filters. Offer a path from failures to the appropriate recovery action.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Open Statistics and compare the queued/ready/processed labels and denominators.
  2. In a disposable environment, interrupt a search request and inspect the resulting message.

Done when: Every stalled/disabled/failed state explains its scope and a useful next step; recoverable errors offer Retry without losing context.

Repository issue: meta/issues/clarify-library-health-and-error-recovery.md

UX-09 / UploadP3

Validate uploads early; make failures recoverable

Design recommendationEffort: S

Unsupported input can reach the upload queue; after submission, failed rows have no targeted recovery action.

What I observed

Browser file-input automation supplied a .txt file alongside a valid WebM. Both entered the pending queue. The server then rejected the .txt and accepted the video, with clear per-file outcomes. This bypassed the native chooser's accept filter; it is not proof the normal chooser lists unsupported files.

Why it matters

The partial-success behavior is good. The remaining friction is learning about obvious invalid files only after submission, and needing to start over to retry a transient failure.

Suggested change

  • Reuse one client-side MIME/extension preflight for drop and picker inputs, while keeping server validation authoritative.
  • Explain rejected files before upload, without adding them to a ready-looking queue.
  • Offer Retry failed for transient failures and a correction/remove action for unsupported formats; preserve successful rows.
  • Use one vocabulary for Upload / Add media / Import and explain duplicate outcomes separately from new uploads.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. In the sandbox, queue an unsupported file and a valid video through browser file-input automation.
  2. Submit and inspect the partial-success summary and available follow-up controls.

Done when: Unsupported drops receive an immediate explanation; a transient failed row can be retried without resubmitting successful files.

Repository issue: meta/issues/063-filter-upload-drop-files-client-side.md

UX-10 / FeedP2

“Back to library” should go to the Library

Reproduced workflow issueEffort: S (exit fix)

The end-of-feed action closes the overlay, returning to the underlying page—even when that page is Settings.

What I observed

Twice in the sandbox: launch Feed from Settings, advance to the last item, click Back to library → the URL remains ?view=settings. Separately, captured mobile Feed shows a truncated title, 0:00 / 0:00 and Pause while metadata is unavailable. Playback did not initialize in this automation environment; no production playback defect is inferred.

Why it matters

The exit label promises a destination it does not deliver. Loading and playback state should also be understandable without interpreting a zero-duration transport.

Suggested change

  • Either navigate to Library or rename the action Close feed / Back to Settings according to the actual destination.
  • Related state improvement: show explicit Loading video / Cannot play states; do not leave an apparently playable zero-duration transport indefinitely.
  • Related layout improvement: keep the video title readable on phones; consider a compact Save control with an accessible label.
  • Handle empty/unplayable launcher outcomes explicitly (existing issue 062); verify playback and gestures on real mobile browsers before changing media logic.
Reproduce / inspect this finding
  1. Open Settings, then start Feed from the rail.
  2. Advance to the terminal item and click Back to library.
  3. Observe that Settings is still the destination.

Done when: The exit action's text matches its destination in every launch context; loading, empty and playback errors are distinguishable.

Repository issue: meta/issues/make-feed-exit-destination-and-loading-state-explicit.md

A direction, not a redesign mandate

One library. Clear task boundaries.

Make browsing, finding, organizing and maintaining feel distinct. Use one vocabulary: media for the mixed library, images/videos for types, collections only for saved lists, and tags for metadata filters. Reserve technical pipeline terms for progressive disclosure.

Suggested mobile structure

Four primary destinations. One search entry. Filters behind a labelled control with an active summary. Utility pages do not inherit the full tag/search band.

Conceptual layout sketch—not a screenshot, not implemented. Preserve the existing visual language.

Library＋
⌕ Search media or choose an image
Filters · Images + videos · NSFW hidden
LibrarySearchCollectionsMore
Approved direction / separate implementation

Yes: retire the legacy UI.

Given the approved retirement direction, make Atelier the single supported shell. Remove the extra destination, but do not confuse removing the shell with removing shared API, authentication or media-serving code.

Small, topical retirement

  1. Remove the legacy rail link, routes and embedded internal/webui/static/ shell. Prefer a clear 404 for retired URLs; add a redirect only if bookmark compatibility is wanted.
  2. Remove the legacy smoke script and npm task; keep Atelier browser tests, Playwright, and shared Go web/media tests.
  3. Update current docs/proxy entries and remove the dead fallback link. Keep historical issues/decisions as history.
  4. Verify root/assets, API/media auth, cookie bootstrapping, MIME/range responses and directory protection.

Do not skip the build gate

A separate architecture inventory found that the CUDA container compiles Go without building Atelier and relies on prebuilt dist. The Atelier smoke script also skips successfully when dist is missing. Retiring legacy without fixing this can leave a clean build with only a placeholder.

Required before removal ships: make supported CI, release and container paths verify that real Atelier assets were built and embedded.

Architecture finding, not a browser-observed production failure. Verified paths: Containerfile.cuda, scripts/ui_smoke_test_atelier.mjs, scripts/package_release.sh, internal/webui/http.go.

Feature disposition—not automatic parity

The inventory found legacy-only bulk image deletion, a retry-stuck-jobs control, and a dedicated tags/live-connection experience. Decide explicitly what to retire and what merits a separate Atelier improvement. I would prioritize a safe retry-failures action and useful tag discovery; I would not block retirement on a new “delete all images” button.

Tracked in meta/issues/retire-legacy-ui-and-require-atelier-build.md. No legacy code was removed in this audit.

Suggested shipping order

Small passes, visible progress.

Trust and safety

Consolidate memberships in manual cleanup (UX-01), correct duplicate certainty/keeper labels (UX-02), guard Settings drafts (UX-05), and fix Feed's return label/destination (UX-10). These are focused changes with clear regression tests.

Orientation and focus

Simplify mobile/desktop navigation (UX-03), make search/tag scope explicit (UX-04), and separate lightbox viewing from editing actions (UX-06). Retire legacy in its own commit once the frontend build gate is reliable.

Organization and recovery

Add collection covers/counts and actionable empty states (UX-07), human-readable health/error states (UX-08), and upload preflight/retry polish (UX-09). Validate the resulting flows on a real phone before expanding gesture or playback work.

Method and limits

What was actually checked

The UI findings came from browser interaction, screenshots, accessibility snapshots and rendered-element measurements—not reading component implementation. A separate source-only inventory informed the legacy-retirement section.

Environment provenance

  • Production: https://imgsearch.home.heldscal.la/, displayed build 907f8a9c433d. Read-only navigation/search; no application mutations.
  • Sandbox: http://127.0.0.1:18081/, repository 2d9b56d, real app/runtime and current embedded frontend; isolated SQLite with foreign keys, safe fixture media, deterministic fake inference and local brute-force index. Fixture search relevance is not representative of production.
  • Browser: agent-browser with Chromium/Chrome for Testing 150, desktop viewport emulation—not a real iOS/Android device. Data counts in screenshots are point-in-time; production annotation continued independently.
  • Media limitation: sandbox HTTP route, MIME, byte ranges, file hash and FFmpeg decode were verified healthy. Browser media elements remained at readyState 0 / unknown duration; root cause was not established. This is not evidence of a server playback regression.
  • Evidence limitation: recording failed at the automation/CDP layer; reproducible before/after screenshots are supplied instead. Blank/transitional captures were excluded from the report.
  • Verification: this is a documentation artifact, so implementation TDD does not apply. Validate embedded assets, internal links, desktop/mobile report rendering and repository checks instead. No fixes, deployment or push are included.

Important distinction: the new opt-in unattended import deduplication in 2d9b56d is separate from the manual Duplicates UI. It was not deployed during this audit, and it does not fix UX-01. Superseded-file retention in that import path should not be implied for manual deletion.
